findings.claim: inOrder keeps scanning after a missing line: the inner loop runs `at` to len(lines) without a match, so every later expected line is also reported as missing. One deleted or reworded rule then produces a cascade of false 'missing' errors, which hides the real cause. The helper should restore `at` or stop at the first miss.

The lint-rule check uses Contains on '\n'+rule+'\n', so it does not pin the line as a whole line the way inOrder does. It also cannot match a rule placed on the first line of the file. It accepts an optional '- ' prefix that the test message does not mention, and it does not check the '## Known errors' heading or its position.

The forbidden-name test matches `(?i)engram` and `gentle-ai` anywhere in the text. A legitimate future mention such as 'engramatic' or a prose reference will fail it. The `\bmem_` pattern is also narrow. The test pins the stated intent only loosely.

The comment says the Claude, OpenCode and Codex adapters write this file into their instruction files. No adapter in this diff reads instructions/owner-rules.md, so the comment describes behavior that does not yet exist and may mislead readers.

evidence: Only two files are added: the rules markdown and its text test. Neither is wired into any adapter in this diff.
The verbatim-rule tests check whole-line equality in order, which matches the commit's claim for the eleven rules, the expertise line and the remote authorization rules.
inOrder's shared index `at` is not reset after a miss, so the first missing line makes every later line fail too.
